title: Yields and prices move opposite ways
objectives: Explain why a bond’s price falls when its yield rises.
Find a yield to maturity by bisection, and rank bonds by sensitivity

screens.title: Same bond, lower price
screens.prose: The 5-year 4% bond was priced at £95.67 when its yield was 5%. Today it trades at £92.00. Its cash flows have not changed.
screens.question: Is its yield now above or below 5%?

options.why: You read a lower price as a lower yield. Paying less for the same cash flows earns you more on each pound.
You treated the yield as fixed when the bond was issued. The yield is set by today's price.
The coupon rate is fixed at 4%; the yield is not. At 4% the price would be £100.

hints.text: At 5% the cash flows are worth £95.67. You now pay less for them.
Paying less for the same money later means a higher return.
A lower price means a higher yield: above 5%.

feedback.correct: Above 5%. Paying less for the same cash flows is a higher return.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You pay less today for exactly the same payments later.

byKey.below: You read a lower price as a lower yield. Paying less for the same cash flows earns you more on each pound.

explain.text: At 5% the cash flows are worth £95.67, more than the £92.00 asked. Only a higher rate discounts them down to £92.00. So the yield is above 5%.

screens.title: Why the price falls
screens.prose: Each bar is one cash flow's value today. Move the yield from 5% to 6% and watch the bars.
screens.question: At a 6% yield, what is the year-5 payment of £104 worth today?

hints.text: Set the yield to 6% and read the Year 5 bar.

feedback.correct: £77.71, down from £81.49 at 5%. The same £104, divided by a bigger number.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move the yield to 6% and read the Year 5 bar.

byKey.at-five: That is its value at 5%. Move the yield to 6%.
byKey.undiscounted: That is the payment itself. Its value today is the payment discounted at 6%.
byKey.price: That is the whole bond at 6%. You want the Year 5 bar alone.

explain.text: The cash flows are fixed, so a higher yield divides each one by a larger number. Every bar shrinks, the far ones most: year 5 loses £3.77. So the price falls when the yield rises.

screens.title: Find the yield
screens.prose: The curve is the bond's price at every yield. Move the yield and watch the price. The dashed line is £92.00.
screens.question: Move the yield until the price is £92.00. What is the yield, to the nearest 0.1%?

hints.text: The price must fall from £95.67 to £92.00. Which way does the yield go?
Watch the dot cross the dashed line.

feedback.correct: About 5.9%. The price fell, so the yield rose.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move the yield until the caption reads about £92.00.

byKey.same: At 5% the price is £95.67. Raise the yield to bring the price down.
byKey.current: That is the coupon over the price, $4/92$. The yield also counts the £100 at maturity.
byKey.lower: You moved the yield down, and the price went up. Move it the other way.

explain.text: At 5.85% the price is £92.15, and at 5.90% it is £91.95. So £92.00 needs a yield of about 5.89%. Along the curve, every rise in yield lowers the price.

screens.title: Halving the interval
screens.prose: You found the bond's **yield to maturity**: the one rate that makes the present value equal the price. Software finds it by **bisection**. Price the midpoint, then keep the half where the price crosses £92.00.
screens.question: Fill in the interval for rows 2 to 4, in percent.

hints.text: If the price at the midpoint is below £92.00, the yield is below the midpoint.
At 6% the price is £91.58, too low, so 6% becomes the high end.
Row 2: 4 to 6, midpoint 5. At £95.67 the price is too high, so row 3 is 5 to 6, midpoint 5.5. Then 5.5 to 6, midpoint 5.75.

feedback.correct: Each row halves the interval. After five rows the yield is pinned between 5.875% and 6%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each midpoint's price with £92.00 to decide which half to keep.

byKey.r1c1: At 6% the price, £91.58, is below £92.00. The yield must be below 6%, so 6% is the new high.
byKey.r2c0: At 5% the price, £95.67, is above £92.00. The yield must be above 5%, so 5% is the new low.
byKey.r3c0: At 5.5% the price, £93.59, is still above £92.00. So 5.5% is the new low.

explain.text: A price above £92.00 means the yield is higher than the midpoint, so the low end moves up. A price below means the high end moves down. Twenty halvings pin the yield to within 0.000004%. Newton's method from the Series and Approximation course gets there in three steps.

screens.title: Duration is the slope
screens.prose: In the Series and Approximation course you found this bond's **modified duration**, $D = 4.40$, from the tangent's slope. For a small yield change, $\Delta P \approx -D\,P\,\Delta y$.
screens.question: By the tangent, how much does the price fall when the yield rises from 5% to 6%?

hints.text: Duration is a percentage of the price per unit of yield.

feedback.correct: £4.21. The true fall, from the curve, is £4.10.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply $D$, the price and $\Delta y$.

byKey.no-price: You took the duration as pounds. It is a percentage: 4.40% of £95.67.
byKey.pct: That is the fraction of the price lost, 4.4%. Multiply by £95.67 for pounds.
byKey.true: That is the true fall, from the curve. The tangent gives a little more.

explain.text: The tangent says $4.40 \times 95.67 \times 0.01 = \text{£}4.21$. The curve bends up, so the true fall is smaller: £4.10. That bend is convexity, 24.47 for this bond.

screens.title: Short and long
screens.prose: Two 4% bonds, one with 2 years left and one with 10. Both yield 5%, and yields rise to 6%.
screens.question: Fill in each bond's percentage change in price.

hints.text: Change is (new − old) / old, as a percentage. Prices fell, so it is negative.

feedback.correct: The 10-year bond loses about four times as much: 7.58% against 1.84%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide each change in price by the price at 5%.

byKey.r0c3: For the 2-year bond, divide $96.33 - 98.14$ by 98.14. Prices fell, so the change is negative.
byKey.r1c3: For the 10-year bond, divide $85.28 - 92.28$ by 92.28. Prices fell, so the change is negative.

explain.text: The 2-year bond falls 1.84% and the 10-year 7.58%. The 10-year's cash flows are further away, so a higher yield discounts them over more years. Its curve is the steeper one: modified duration 7.96 against 1.87.

screens.title: A bond with one payment
screens.prose: A zero-coupon bond's value all arrives at maturity $T$. So its **Macaulay duration**, the average time of its cash flows weighted by present value, is exactly $T$. Modified duration divides that by $1 + y$.
screens.question: What is the modified duration of a 5-year zero-coupon bond at a 5% yield?

hints.text: Its Macaulay duration is its maturity, 5 years.
Modified duration is Macaulay duration divided by $1 + y$.

feedback.correct: 4.76, more than the coupon bond's 4.40. With no coupons, all the value waits until year 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the maturity by 1.05.

byKey.macaulay: 5 is the Macaulay duration. Divide by $1 + y$ for the modified duration.
byKey.coupon: 4.40 is the 4% coupon bond. The zero has no early cash flows to pull its duration down.

explain.text: $D = 5/1.05 = 4.76$, against 4.40 for the 4% bond of the same maturity. Coupons return money early and shorten duration. So a lower coupon means more sensitivity, and a zero is the extreme.

screens.title: Is a higher yield good news?
screens.prose: You bought the 5-year 4% bond for £95.67 at a 5% yield. Overnight, yields rise to 6%. A friend says you are better off, because your bond now yields 6%.
screens.question: What has happened to the value of your bond?

options.text: You are better off: it now yields 6%
options.why: You read the higher yield as a gain to you. The 6% goes to whoever buys at today's lower price.

options.text: Nothing: its coupons and face value are fixed
options.why: The cash flows are fixed, but their value today is not. At 6% they are worth less.
That is a fall in yields, to 4%. Yields rose, so the price fell.

hints.text: Read the price at 6% on the curve.
Your bond's cash flows are now discounted at 6%.
At 6% the price is £91.58, down £4.10.

feedback.correct: £4.10 down. A new buyer earns 6% from £91.58; you have already lost the difference.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price your bond's fixed cash flows at the new 6% yield.

byKey.better: You read the higher yield as a gain to you. The 6% goes to whoever buys at today's lower price.
byKey.fixed: The cash flows are fixed, but their value today is not. At 6% they are worth £4.10 less.

explain.text: Your cash flows are fixed, so a 6% yield prices them at £91.58. You have lost £4.10 today. If you hold to maturity you still earn your 5%; the 6% belongs to the new buyer.

screens.title: Current yield
screens.prose: Quotes often show the **current yield** too: the annual coupon divided by the price. It ignores the gain or loss at maturity.
screens.question: What is its current yield?

hints.text: Divide the coupon by the price.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the £4 coupon by the £95.67 price.

byKey.ytm: That is the yield to maturity, which also counts the £4.33 rise to £100 at the end.
byKey.coupon: That is the coupon over the face value. Divide by the price instead.
byKey.inverse: That is the £4.33 pull to £100 over the price. The current yield uses the coupon.

explain.text: The current yield is $4/95.67 = 4.18\%$. The yield to maturity is higher, 5%. It also counts the £4.33 the bond gains on its way to £100. For a premium bond the order flips.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose:
Price is a falling curve in the yield, and it bends upwards. For a small move,
$$\Delta P \approx -D\,P\,\Delta y$$
so a bigger $D$ means more sensitivity. Longer maturities and lower coupons push cash flows later and raise $D$.
screens.question: Yields rise 1% for all four bonds. Which loses the largest share of its price?

options.why: Its large coupons return money early, which shortens its duration.
Its cash flows are close, so they are discounted over few years.
No coupons helps, but 2 years is short. Its duration is under 2.

feedback.correct: The 10-year zero: the longest maturity and no coupons. Its modified duration is $10/1.05 = 9.52$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the latest cash flows.

explain.text: The 10-year zero has all its value at year 10, so $D = 10/1.05 = 9.52$. The 8% 10-year bond's coupons pull its duration well below that. Both 2-year bonds have durations under 2.

screens.title: A portfolio's risk
screens.prose: You run a £10 million bond portfolio with a modified duration of 4.4. The central bank surprises the market, and yields rise 1 percentage point across the board.
screens.question: About how much does the portfolio lose?

hints.text: Use $\Delta P \approx -D\,P\,\Delta y$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the duration, the value and the yield change as a decimal.

byKey.tenth: You used a 0.1% move. One percentage point is $\Delta y = 0.01$.
byKey.no-pct: You multiplied by 1 instead of 0.01. A 1% move is $\Delta y = 0.01$.
byKey.one-pct: You took 1% of the value. Duration multiplies that: 4.4 times as much.

explain.text: $4.4 \times \text{£}10{,}000{,}000 \times 0.01 = \text{£}440{,}000$. Convexity makes the true loss a little smaller. If the portfolio were the 5-year 4% bond, it would lose £428,058.

screens.prose: In 2022 central banks raised interest rates fast to fight inflation, and bond yields jumped. A broad index of US investment-grade bonds lost about 13% that year, its worst year on record. Almost every bond in it kept paying its coupons.
screens.question: What mostly explains the loss?

options.text: Higher yields discounted the same fixed cash flows harder, so prices fell
Many of the bonds defaulted and stopped paying
options.why: You looked for missed payments. Almost every bond paid in full; the loss came from prices.

options.text: The bonds cut their coupons when rates rose
options.why: A bond's coupon is fixed when it is issued. Rising rates do not change it.

options.text: Nothing real: higher yields made the bonds better
options.why: You read the higher yield as good news for holders. It is good for new buyers, at lower prices.

hints.text: What happens to a bond's price when its yield rises?
Duration links a yield change to a price change.
Fixed cash flows discounted at higher yields are worth less: prices fell.

feedback.correct: Yields up, prices down. Funds holding long bonds, with high durations, fell most.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what a rise in yield does to a fixed cash flow's value today.

explain.text: Rising yields cut the present value of every fixed coupon and face value. With durations of about six years, a rise of a couple of points means losses in the teens. Holders to maturity still get every pound; the loss is on today's price.

ideas: The yield to maturity is the one rate that makes the present value of the cash flows equal the price. Bisection or Newton finds it.
The cash flows are fixed, so a higher yield discounts them harder: price falls as yield rises, along a curve that bends up.
Modified duration is the slope per pound: $\Delta P \approx -D\,P\,\Delta y$. Longer maturity and lower coupons raise $D$; a zero's Macaulay duration is its maturity.

formula.name: Price change from duration
formula.note: Good for small moves; for large ones the curve's upward bend makes the true fall smaller.

summary.trap: A higher yield is not good news for a holder: it means the bond's price has fallen.

quiz.prose: A bond's yield falls from 6% to 5%. Nothing else changes.
quiz.question: What happens to its price?

options.why: You moved price and yield together. A lower yield discounts the same cash flows less, so the price rises.

options.text: It stays the same: the coupons are fixed
options.why: The cash flows are fixed, but their value today depends on the yield.

feedback.correct: It rises. Price and yield move opposite ways.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A lower yield divides each cash flow by a smaller number.

explain.text: Each cash flow is divided by $(1+y)^t$. A smaller $y$ makes every divisor smaller, so every present value, and the price, rises.

quiz.prose: A bond is priced at £102.00 with a modified duration of 7.0. Its yield rises by 0.5 percentage points.
quiz.question: About how much does its price fall?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply duration, price and $\Delta y = 0.005$.

byKey.no-price: That is the percentage, 3.5. Multiply it by the £102 price.
byKey.full-pct: You used a 1-point move. Half a point is $\Delta y = 0.005$.
byKey.fraction: That is the fraction of the price, 0.035. Multiply by £102.

explain.text: $\Delta P \approx -D\,P\,\Delta y = -7.0 \times 102 \times 0.005 = -3.57$. The price falls about £3.57.

quiz.prose: A bond pays a £6 annual coupon and is priced at £105.00. Its yield to maturity is 4.9%.
quiz.question: What is its current yield, in percent?

feedback.correct: 5.71%. Here it is above the yield to maturity, because the bond loses £5 on its way to £100.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the coupon by the price.

byKey.coupon: That is the coupon over the face value. Divide by the £105 price.
byKey.ytm: That is the yield to maturity. The current yield is the coupon over the price.

explain.text: $6/105 = 5.71\%$. A premium bond falls to £100 by maturity, so its yield to maturity, 4.9%, is below its current yield.

quiz.prose: The 5-year 4% bond, at £95.67 with modified duration 4.40, sees yields jump from 5% to 8%. Duration alone predicts a fall of 13.2%.
quiz.question: How does the true fall compare?

options.text: Smaller, about 12.2%, because the price curve bends up
The same, 13.2%: duration gives the change
options.why: You treated the curve as a straight line. Over 3 points its bend matters.

options.text: Bigger, because large moves hurt more than duration says
options.why: You expected the bend to add to the loss. The curve bends up, so it cushions a fall.

feedback.correct: The true price is £84.03, a fall of 12.2%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Does the curve lie above or below its tangent?

explain.text: The true price at 8% is £84.03, a 12.2% fall; the tangent gives £83.04. The curve bends up, so a straight line overstates large falls. Convexity, 24.47 here, corrects most of the gap.
